summary.text: The Pacific decadal oscillation is a recurring pattern of ocean and air climate swings, seen as warm or cool surface water in the Pacific north of 20°N.
In its warm phase the west Pacific cools and part of the eastern ocean warms, the cool phase does the reverse, and its strength has varied over a few years to several decades.
It affects coastal sea and air temperatures from Alaska to California, and its last two flips lined up with sharp shifts in North Pacific salmon production.

facts.label: Region tracked
facts.value: North Pacific surface waters, north of 20°N

facts.label: Long rhythm
facts.value: A 50–70 year periodicity in the reconstructed index

items.prompt: The Pacific decadal oscillation was first noticed in 1997 by a researcher poring over records of what?

options.label: Coral reef bleaching in the tropics
Old ship logbooks of sea temperature
Salmon production in the North Pacific
Snowfall totals in the Rocky Mountains

items.explain: Steven R. Hare named the pattern after noticing it while studying salmon production results in 1997.

items.prompt: The oscillation has just swung into its warm, positive phase. What does the Pacific's surface look like?

options.label: The west turns cooler while part of the east warms
The whole ocean warms evenly from west to east
The west warms while the eastern side cools
Only waters near the equator change at all

items.explain: In the warm phase the west Pacific becomes cooler and part of the eastern ocean warms; the cool phase flips this.

items.prompt: During a positive phase, the winter Aleutian Low deepens and warm, humid air flows up the North American west coast. Which region is likely warmer than usual?

options.label: Mexico
The Southeastern United States
Florida and the Gulf coast
The Pacific Northwest and Alaska

items.explain: In the positive phase temperatures run higher than usual from the Pacific Northwest to Alaska but below normal in Mexico and the Southeastern United States.

items.prompt: A patch of unusually warm water forms in the North Pacific one winter, disappears from the surface in summer, then shows up again the next winter. Why?

options.label: Summer sunlight heats the same spot again
It hid below the shallow summer surface layer
Currents carry it to Asia and straight back
Satellites cannot see the ocean in summer

items.explain: Winter anomalies reach down through the deep winter mixed layer, get sealed beneath the shallow summer layer, and resurface when it deepens again, the reemergence mechanism.

items.prompt: How does the way the Pacific decadal oscillation arises differ from El Niño–Southern Oscillation?

options.label: It is driven only by changes in the Sun
It is a single ocean mode with one cause
It is a sum of several processes, not one mode
It happens only in the Southern Hemisphere

items.explain: Unlike ENSO, the PDO is not a single physical mode of ocean variability but the sum of several processes with different origins.

items.prompt: Reliable instrument records cover only about a century, yet the oscillation has been traced back to the year 993. What made that possible?

options.label: Satellite images of ancient sea ice
Thermometer logs kept by medieval monks
Fish bones found in coastal villages
Tree rings from California and Alberta

items.explain: MacDonald and Case reconstructed the index back to 993 using tree rings from California and Alberta.

paragraphs.heading: A slow swing in the North Pacific
paragraphs.text: The Pacific decadal oscillation, or PDO, is a recurring pattern of climate swings in both the ocean and the air over the middle-latitude Pacific. It shows up as unusually warm or cool surface water in the Pacific north of 20°N. Its reach goes beyond the sea: it changes coastal sea temperatures and air temperatures over the land from Alaska down to California.

paragraphs.heading: Warm and cool phases
paragraphs.text: In its warm, or positive, phase the western Pacific cools and part of the eastern ocean warms; in its cool, or negative, phase the reverse happens. Over the past century its strength has wandered irregularly, over spans from a few years to several decades. The pattern seems to have flipped around 1925, 1947 and 1977, and the last two flips lined up with sharp changes in North Pacific salmon production. Fittingly, Steven R. Hare noticed and named the pattern in 1997 while studying salmon production results.

paragraphs.heading: Many causes, one index
paragraphs.text: The PDO index is built from monthly sea surface temperature anomalies across the North Pacific, after the global average has been taken out. Several studies suggest the index is a blend of tropical forcing and processes from outside the tropics. That sets it apart from El Niño: the PDO is not one physical mode of the ocean but the sum of several processes with different origins. Over a few years, it is made of random swings plus El Niño-driven changes in the Aleutian Low, while over decades, El Niño links, random weather and changes in the North Pacific gyre circulation each add roughly equal parts.

paragraphs.heading: An ocean memory
paragraphs.text: Surface temperature patterns can persist from winter to winter through what is called the reemergence mechanism, a name given by Alexander and Deser. In winter the ocean's mixed layer over the North Pacific is deep, typically 100–200m. An anomaly that forms in winter and reaches that deep gets trapped under the thin summer mixed layer when it reforms in late spring, cut off from heat exchange with the air. When the mixed layer deepens again in the next autumn or early winter, the old anomaly can reach the surface once more. So patterns tend to return the next winter while skipping the summer between.

paragraphs.heading: What it does to weather
paragraphs.text: In the positive phase, the winter Aleutian Low deepens and moves south, and warm, humid air flows along the west coast of North America. Temperatures then run above normal from Alaska down to the Pacific Northwest, but below normal in Mexico and the south-eastern United States. Together with the Atlantic multidecadal oscillation, the PDO strongly shapes decades-long drought in the United States. When the Atlantic pattern is positive, droughts are more frequent over much of the northern states in the positive PDO phase and over the Southwest in the negative phase. The Asian monsoon feels it as well, with more rain and cooler summers over the Indian subcontinent in the negative phase.

paragraphs.heading: Read in tree rings
paragraphs.text: Tree rings let scientists trace the PDO far into the past. One reconstruction based on tree-ring records from the Baja California area reaches back to 1661, and MacDonald and Case pushed it to the year 993 using trees from California and Alberta. Their record shows a rhythm of 50 to 70 years, though the pattern is only strong after 1800. Through a warm medieval period, from 993 to 1300, the PDO stayed in a negative phase, which fits with droughts lasting centuries in the US Southwest.
